newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria sets cautious coalition in place.
newsitem.headline: Algeria sets cautious coalition in place.

text.p: Algeria has put in place a coalition government to try to end years of violence, cautiously bringing more moderate Islamists into power but ensuring most key posts stay with former ministers loyal to President Liamine Zeroual.
Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia, whose team had to be approved by Zeroual, brought back his foreign, finance, interior and other ministers in the three-party coalition.

Explaining why much of the old team had been reappointed, and underlying the task ahead, one of the ministers said: "We have succeeded in breaking the 'cordon' around Algeria that has been there for several years. But it is not finished as there is still some resistance."
Youssef Yousfi, a former head of Zeroual's cabinet and deputy president of the state oil and gas giant Sonatrach was brought into the vital post of energy minister.
OPEC member Algeria relies on oil and gas exports for more than 90 percent of its foreign revenue.
Analysts saw the new government, announced late on Wednesday, as an attempt to broaden the political base of the president, a former general.
It was also designed to maintain the momentum of economic reforms, and to try to show the country's 29 million people the government was for all segments of society.
Radical Islamists, whose domination of Algeria's first multi- party general election in December 1991 led the authorities to scrap the poll, were barred from contesting the June ballot.
But two moderate Islamist-leaning parties were authorised and between them took 103 seats in the 380-seat National Assembly.

The lineup of 28 ministers, including Ouyahia, three junior ministers and eight secretaries of state, includes representatives of National Liberation Front (FLN) which ran Algeria for nearly three decades.

The party which dominated the election -- the National Democratic Rally (RND) was formed only two months before the poll. It attracted Zeroual's staunchest supporters, with many outgoing ministers, including Ouyahia, standing as candidates under its banner.
The RND, MPS and FLN emerged as the most popular parties in the election, winning respectively 156, 69 and 62 seats in the 380-member lower house.

Incumbent Foreign, Interior, Finance and Trade Ministers -- respectively Ahmed Attaf, Mustapaha Benmansour, Abdelkrim Harchaoui and Bakhti Belaid -- were reappointed. Zeroual, following normal Algerian tradition, keeps the defence portfolio.
MPS's main leaders Bougerra Soltani, know as Abu Jarra, and Abdelmajid Menasra were named respectively Small and Medium Enterprise Minister and Industry Minister.
Other MPS officials were appointed as junior ministers.

The FLN took some ministries and secretary of state posts, but the influential War Veterans ministry remained with Said Abadou, and the important economic post of telecommunications minister stayed in the hands of incumbent Mohamed Salah Youyou.
Other ministers to be reappointed were Justice Minister Mohamed Adami and National Solidarity Minister Mrs Rabea Mechernene, whose post was upgraded to full minister.

The perceived lack of substantial change could sour some support for the authorities. Anti-Islamists, for example, have no direct voice in the government, their two parties saying they would not take part in a coalition with Islamists and the FLN.

Diplomats earlier this month said the abstention rate of about 35 percent in the June 5 poll suggested widespread disillusionment with the lack of change brought about by Zeroual and said the new government lineup could be crucial to the country's future.
One analyst at the time said the worst case scenario would be a coalition government limited to the RND and the FLN.
"Most Algerians...will read that as proof that the regime has decided to block efforts to forge an alternative to the status quo," he said.

About 60,000 people have died in the violence since the aborted election nearly six years ago, and Zeroual sees this new election -- to be followed by local elections this year -- as an important step to ending the nation's crisis.
